title: East and south
hookLine: parents and children, teachers and students: duties both ways
carry: respect flows up, care flows down

lines: FROM THE YOUNG TO THE OLD.
cards: Honor your father and mother. Respect your elders. Listen to your teacher.
Rules like these point one way: from the young to the old. The Sigalovada does something worth noticing. Every time it tells the young man what he owes, it turns around and says what is owed to him.
Five duties going one way, five coming back, for parents and for teachers alike. A bow in two directions.

teach.b: East is the parents, the direction where the day begins. A child, the Buddha says, honors them in five ways, thinking: they supported me, so I'll support them. I'll do the work they need done.
I'll keep up the family line. I'll be worthy of what they leave me. And when they've died, I'll make offerings in their memory.
Parents, honored like this, show their love in five ways too.

They keep their child from what's harmful, encourage what's good, have the child trained in a skill, help arrange a suitable marriage, and at the right time, hand over the inheritance. South is the teachers.
A student honors a teacher by rising to greet them, by waiting on them, by being eager to learn, by small acts of service, and by taking the lesson seriously.

teach.h: TEACHERS: THE WHOLE CRAFT, AND SAFETY.
teach.b: The teacher in return trains the student well, makes sure they've really understood, teaches them the whole of the craft, speaks well of them to friends, and keeps them safe wherever they go. Notice the balance.

The child's list ends with remembering parents after death; the parents' list ends with letting go of what they own at the right time. The student's list ends with attention; the teacher's with protection.
Some details belong to ancient India, arranged marriages and inheritances. But the shape is plain. Respect flows up, care flows down, and when both flow, the direction is honored.

how: In some Buddhist countries children bow to their parents and students to their teachers at festivals such as Thailand's teacher-honoring ceremony, and families make offerings and merit in memory of parents who have died.

o: a duty owed to one's parents
a direction, like east or south
a ritual bath taken at sunrise

games.q: east and south: tap the pairs.

s: the Sigalovada lists duties only from children to parents
five duties go each way: parents owe their children too.
one duty of parents is to have their child trained in a skill
along with guarding, encouraging, marriage and inheritance.
a good teacher in DN 31 speaks well of the student to friends
and teaches the whole of the craft.

games.q: you're a teacher in the Sigalovada. your student has risen to greet you and is eager to learn. what do you owe back?
o: train them well, teach the whole craft, speak well of them and keep them safe.
games.why: the teacher owes five duties in return, ending with keeping the student safe wherever they go.

practice: Turn, if you can, toward the east and bring to mind a parent, or whoever raised you, living or not, and quietly honor one thing they gave you.
Then turn toward the south and bring to mind a teacher, a coach, a mentor, someone who showed you how, and let one lesson they gave you come up.
If you have children or students yourself, notice the duties coming back the other way.

wordCard.voice: disa. In DN 31 the east is parents and the south is teachers, each with five duties owed and five returned. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali puratthima disa: the eastern direction, which DN 31 gives to parents.

carryVoice: Your line: respect flows up, care flows down. Five duties each way, for parents and for teachers. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the eastern and southern directions
